# Pull Request Information - **PR #**: 1247 - **URL**: https://github.com/IstiN/flutter_agent_harness/pull/1247 - **Title**: gh-1073 Session JSONL grows unboundedly (12 GiB ledger records) → resume fails with 'Failed to read session' + heap-exhaustion crash - **Author**: ai-teammate - **Branch**: `ai/gh-1073` → `main` - **State**: open - **Files Changed**: 29 - **Additions**: +4680 - **Deletions**: -60 - **Created**: 2026-10-04T21:28:28Z - **Updated**: 2026-10-04T22:14:31Z ## PR Description ### What changed Bounded the session-JSONL growth that grew a month-long session to 12.4 GiB and made open/resume safe for huge files: ledger payloads are capped and deduped at the write site, the full open streams the file in bounded chunks (never one giant `String`) with a 2 GiB hard backstop, and a new `fa session repair` command rewrites bloated JSONLs. This leg fixed the last review leftovers: one analyzer lint and two stale retry-test assertions that still counted the old `readTextFile` open surface (the open now stats + streams, so the counters read `statCalls`). ### Key decisions - `ledger_caps.dart`: 300-char cap on every string field in `shell_job_registry` / `subagent_registry` records + `LedgerSnapshotDeduper` skips byte-identical snapshots at the write site - `model_request_summary`: per-message summaries capped (newest 64 messages / 256 KB budget); older messages degrade to role+chars stubs — record still describes the whole request - `JsonlSessionStorage._openLocked`: stat-first, refuse >2 GiB with a named `tooLarge` `SessionException` pointing at windowed resume / `fa session repair`; ranged filesystems get a fully streamed line-scan parse with header-only decode of giant `custom` ledgers (only the latest per `customType` is fully parsed — exactly what resume rehydration reads) - `session_repair.dart` + CLI: drop replay-only ledger types, keep-latest for snapshot registries, conservative (unknown/unparseable lines kept), backup + `--dry-run` ### How to verify ```bash dart test test/session test/trajectory test/task test/cli ``` Full core suite (`dart test --exclude-tags integration`): 7960 passed / 16 skipped. The 3 failures in `providers_queue_editor_test.dart` are environmental — the CI shell leaks `FA_PROVIDERS_QUEUE`, which the editor correctly refuses to override (all 13 pass with the var unset). A pre-existing glibc heap-corruption abort in the PTY-harness teardown also reproduces on the base commit and is unrelated.

bounded chunks] STREAM --> HDR[header-only decode
of giant custom ledgers] HDR --> LATEST[fully parse latest
record per customType] WRITE[ledger writes] --> CAP[ledger_caps: 300-char field cap] CAP --> DEDUP[skip identical snapshots] REPAIR[fa session repair] --> REWRITE[drop replay-only ledgers
keep-latest registries + backup] ```

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the live-session guard is skipped for direct `.jsonl` path targets**

The by-id branch below correctly refuses to repair a session with a fresh presence heartbeat ("repairing under a writer loses appends"), and both this file's doc comment and the `cli_help.dart` entry promise "A live session (fresh heartbeat) is refused" unconditionally. But when the target ends in `.jsonl`, this branch takes `path = target` and **never checks presence** — `fa session repair /live/session.jsonl` on a running session will scan, rewrite, and swap the file under the writer, silently dropping every append between the scan and the rename.

The fix is cheap: run the same `presenceStore` lookup for the path branch. Resolving a path to a session id would need a listing scan, but even a simpler guard helps — e.g. refuse when *any* fresh heartbeat row names this path, or at minimum rename the option/document it as an unsafe expert escape hatch. As written, the doc comment overpromises and the most dangerous input shape is the least protected one.

💡 **SUGGESTION: the board snapshot is serialized twice, and the deduper marks state persisted before the write succeeds**

Two small things in this hunk:

1. `_jobBoard.toRecords()` is called twice and the payload is JSON-encoded twice — once here for the dedupe key, once inside `appendCustomEntry`. With the new 50-card cap that's cheap, but `final records = _jobBoard.toRecords(); final json = jsonEncode(records);` makes the dedupe key honestly match what gets written.
2. `LedgerSnapshotDeduper.shouldPersist` advances `_lastJson` before the append runs. The chain's `.catchError` swallows append failures by design — but then the deduper believes the snapshot persisted, so the retried *identical* snapshot is skipped and the ledger silently misses a state until the next mutation. Consider rolling the deduper back on write failure (e.g. `shouldPersist` returning a token the catch path can restore), or documenting the at-most-one-lost-snapshot window.

💡 **SUGGESTION: double newline when quarantining torn lines**

The torn span's `end` already includes the line's trailing `\n` (see `SessionScannedLine.byteLength` — "trailing newline included"), so `$text` here already ends with `\n` and appending `'$text\n'` writes a stray blank line after every quarantined record in the `.corrupt` sidecar. Harmless for forensics, but the sidecar then no longer round-trips as one-record-per-line. Append `$text` (or strip the newline and add it back) so the sidecar stays clean JSONL.

💡 **SUGGESTION: `test/dbg_heal_test.dart` looks like a committed debug leftover**

The `dbg_` filename, five `print` calls (each needing an `avoid_print` ignore), and — most importantly — **zero `expect` assertions** mark this as scaffolding from diagnosing the header-less heal path rather than a regression test. It does still exercise the path (a throw would fail), so either give it real assertions (e.g. expect the healed header, the quarantine sidecar content, and `reopened` entry ids) and rename it into `test/session/`, or drop it — as-is it just adds log noise to the suite.

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the live-session guard is skipped for direct `.jsonl` path targets**

The by-id branch below correctly refuses to repair a session with a fresh presence heartbeat ("repairing under a writer loses appends"), and both this file's doc comment and the `cli_help.dart` entry promise "A live session (fresh heartbeat) is refused" unconditionally. But when the target ends in `.jsonl`, this branch takes `path = target` and **never checks presence** — `fa session repair /live/session.jsonl` on a running session will scan, rewrite, and swap the file under the writer, silently dropping every append between the scan and the rename.

The fix is cheap: run the same `presenceStore` lookup for the path branch. Resolving a path to a session id would need a listing scan, but even a simpler guard helps — e.g. refuse when *any* fresh heartbeat row names this path, or at minimum rename the option/document it as an unsafe expert escape hatch. As written, the doc comment overpromises and the most dangerous input shape is the least protected one.

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: the board snapshot is serialized twice, and the deduper marks state persisted before the write succeeds**

Two small things in this hunk:

1. `_jobBoard.toRecords()` is called twice and the payload is JSON-encoded twice — once here for the dedupe key, once inside `appendCustomEntry`. With the new 50-card cap that's cheap, but `final records = _jobBoard.toRecords(); final json = jsonEncode(records);` makes the dedupe key honestly match what gets written.
2. `LedgerSnapshotDeduper.shouldPersist` advances `_lastJson` before the append runs. The chain's `.catchError` swallows append failures by design — but then the deduper believes the snapshot persisted, so the retried *identical* snapshot is skipped and the ledger silently misses a state until the next mutation. Consider rolling the deduper back on write failure (e.g. `shouldPersist` returning a token the catch path can restore), or documenting the at-most-one-lost-snapshot window.

5. Potential bug: `latestGiantCustoms` map is keyed by customType but the rehydration loop at the end fully parses `rawLine` and replaces entry by id — good. But note: the map only holds the LATEST across segments because later writes overwrite — since segments scanned oldest-first, later segments win. But within a segment, later lines overwrite earlier — latest wins. Good. However if the same customType appears in a later segment but is NOT giant there (small record, data != null), the older giant rawLine remains in the map and gets fully parsed and replaces... wait, the small record in the later segment would have been added to entries with data != null and seenRecordIds.add. Then the older giant rawLine's full parse would replace... no — the full parse replaces the entry with `entries[indexWhere(e.id == full.id)]` — the giant record's id, which would be the entry in entries from the older segment (first copy wins dedupe). Hmm, but if a newer SMALL record of same type exists in a later segment, the stale giant from earlier segment would still be rehydrated and take precedence in the entries list, while resume rehydration reads "the latest per customType" from entries — which would then be the old giant rather than the new small record. Edge case; probably fine because dedupe and ordering mean the latest record of that type should be the last entry in entries with that customType. Actually rehydration reads latest entry per customType from entries — if old giant entry appears later in the list? No, older segment entries come first. So the latest entry with that customType would be the new small one. OK.

But wait — there's a subtle bug: blank lines skipped means their spans are excluded from both good and torn spans; the rewrite copies only goodSpans, so blank lines disappear. OK, fine.

If it fails because backup exists, repair fails. Check the local fs renamePath behavior. Possibly overwrites on POSIX (rename(2) replaces). OK.

When the target is a `.jsonl` path (`target.endsWith('.jsonl')`), the presence check is **skipped entirely** — repairing a live session by path is allowed and will lose appends. That's a real inconsistency. Severity: IMPORTANT (data-loss risk on a documented path, but requires explicit path usage; still the guard exists and is bypassed). Given "when in doubt, start one level higher" and data loss is possible — could argue BLOCKING? The verdict rules: BLOCKING = correctness/bug/data loss. Repairing under a live writer loses data. But the by-path branch is arguably "advanced" usage. Hmm. The guard's own comment says "repairing under a writer loses appends" — and the by-id branch enforces it. The by-path branch silently skips it. I'd call this IMPORTANT (strong) or BLOCKING. Data loss is explicitly listed under BLOCKING. But is it a bug? Yes — inconsistent guard. I'll classify IMPORTANT-to-BLOCKING... Let me decide: the CLI resolves sessions two ways; one checks live, one doesn't. A user repairing "the file directly" would reasonably still be protected. The comment in the doc says "A session owned by a LIVE process (fresh presence heartbeat) is refused" — as a blanket statement, which is false for the path branch. I'll mark it BLOCKING? The machine: any BLOCKING → REQUEST_CHANGES. This is a genuine correctness issue in a data-loss direction. But it's also plausible the author intended path = expert mode. Still, the doc comment promises refusal. I lean IMPORTANT with a strong note, since the primary flow is guarded and path-based repair is an explicit escape hatch... but "repairing under a writer loses appends" applies equally. Data loss risk + doc mismatch → I'll go with BLOCKING. Hmm, let me weigh: review guidelines say "When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible." Risk: user runs `fa session repair <path>.jsonl` while session is live → appends lost silently. Not negligible. BLOCKING.

```dart
if (entry is CustomRecord &&
```

`entry.data == null` also matches a genuine custom record with null data (not shallow-parsed, e.g. a small record... no, small records have data; but a custom record that legitimately has `data: null` and line < threshold won't match due to length check). But: a giant custom record where `shallowCustomHeader` returned null (foreign field order) gets fully parsed with real data → entry.data != null → not added to latestGiantCustoms. Fine.

But a real edge: a giant `custom` record with data==null that is NOT a ledger — e.g. some custom type where data is legitimately null. Then latestGiantCustoms[customType] = rawLine and at rehydration it's fully parsed with parseSessionEntryLine — result has data==null anyway. Fine.

Rehydration loop: `final full = parseSessionEntryLine(rawLine, filePath, 0);` — uses `filePath` (primary path) as filePath param even for records from part segments; error messages would name the wrong file. Cosmetic.

Blank lines: skipped, not counted in batchFirstLineNumber... batchFirstLineNumber increments only by batchLines.length (non-blank). Line numbers in error messages will drift from actual file lines when blank lines present. Pre-existing semantics likely similar in whole-file path? Minor.

{"content":"⚠️ **IMPORTANT: the live-session guard is skipped for direct `.jsonl` path targets**

The by-id branch below correctly refuses to repair a session with a fresh presence heartbeat ("repairing under a writer loses appends"), and both this file's doc comment and the `cli_help.dart` entry promise "A live session (fresh heartbeat) is refused" unconditionally. But when the target ends in `.jsonl`, this branch takes `path = target` and **never checks presence** — `fa session repair /live/session.jsonl` on a running session will scan, rewrite, and swap the file under the writer, silently dropping every append between the scan and the rename.

The fix is cheap: run the same `presenceStore` lookup for the path branch. Resolving a path to a session id would need a listing scan, but even a simpler guard helps — e.g. refuse when *any* fresh heartbeat row names this path, or at minimum rename the option/document it as an unsafe expert escape hatch. As written, the doc comment overpromises and the most dangerous input shape is the least protected one.

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: the board snapshot is serialized twice, and the deduper marks state persisted before the write succeeds**

Two small things in this hunk:

1. `_jobBoard.toRecords()` is called twice and the payload is JSON-encoded twice — once here for the dedupe key, once inside `appendCustomEntry`. With the new 50-card cap that's cheap, but `final records = _jobBoard.toRecords(); final json = jsonEncode(records);` makes the dedupe key honestly match what gets written.
2. `LedgerSnapshotDeduper.shouldPersist` advances `_lastJson` before the append runs. The chain's `.catchError` swallows append failures by design — but then the deduper believes the snapshot persisted, so the retried *identical* snapshot is skipped and the ledger silently misses a state until the next mutation. Consider rolling the deduper back on write failure (e.g. `shouldPersist` returning a token the catch path can restore), or documenting the at-most-one-lost-snapshot window.

All required context — ticket description, PR diff, CI status, and related materials — has already been prepared in the `input/` folder. Do not ask for identifiers; the context is already available locally. ```mermaid flowchart TD G1["⚠️ Review Guidelines — evaluate against existing codebase patterns"] G2["Before reviewing, explore the project's code structure, architecture, and testing patterns"] G3["If AGENTS.md exists → READ it — defines coding styles to check against"] G4["Flag deviations from established patterns unless justified in PR description"] G1 --> G2 --> G3 --> G4 ``` # PR Review General Guidelines ## Review flow ```mermaid flowchart TD START([PR ready for review]) --> READ["1. Read input context:
instruction.md, ticket.md, pr_info.md,

Test coverage · Duplication · Backward compatibility"] DIMS --> SEVERITY["6. Classify each finding:
BLOCKING / IMPORTANT / SUGGESTION"] SEVERITY --> EXHAUST["7. Exhaustive pass:
re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Review dimensions Rate the PR across all relevant dimensions: | Dimension | What to check | |---|---| | **Security** | injection, unsafe interpolation, secret leakage, missing permissions, unsafe defaults | | **Architecture / OOP** | SRP, coupling, abstraction consistency, provider/repository boundaries | | **Code quality** | naming, complexity, error handling, logging, comments | | **Tests** | coverage for new/changed paths, meaningful assertions, no brittle string-only tests | | **Duplication** | copy-paste, duplicated logic across files, duplicated configuration | | **Backward compatibility** | public API changes, migration paths, default behavior | | **Performance** | unnecessary rebuilds, heavy sync operations, missing timeouts | | **Workflow / CI safety** | (when `.github/workflows/` changes) secret declarations, ref pinning, permissions, timeouts | ## 6. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. Outputs Write the standard review artifacts: - `outputs/pr_review.json` — structured data with `recommendation`, `summary`, `inlineComments`, `issueCounts` - `outputs/pr_review_general.md` — 1-2 paragraph general PR comment - `outputs/pr_review_comments/*.md` — one file per detailed inline comment **Inline comment lines must be present in the PR diff.** GitHub review threads can only be attached to added or context lines inside a diff hunk. Findings on unchanged code outside the diff belong in `outputs/pr_review_general.md`, not as inline comments. # Pull Request Information - **PR #**: 1247 - **URL**: https://github.com/IstiN/flutter_agent_harness/pull/1247 - **Title**: gh-1073 Session JSONL grows unboundedly (12 GiB ledger records) → resume fails with 'Failed to read session' + heap-exhaustion crash - **Author**: ai-teammate - **Branch**: `ai/gh-1073` → `main` - **State**: open - **Files Changed**: 29 - **Additions**: +4680 - **Deletions**: -60 - **Created**: 2026-10-04T21:28:28Z - **Updated**: 2026-10-04T22:14:31Z ## PR Description ### What changed Bounded the session-JSONL growth that grew a month-long session to 12.4 GiB and made open/resume safe for huge files: ledger payloads are capped and deduped at the write site, the full open streams the file in bounded chunks (never one giant `String`) with a 2 GiB hard backstop, and a new `fa session repair` command rewrites bloated JSONLs. This leg fixed the last review leftovers: one analyzer lint and two stale retry-test assertions that still counted the old `readTextFile` open surface (the open now stats + streams, so the counters read `statCalls`). ### Key decisions - `ledger_caps.dart`: 300-char cap on every string field in `shell_job_registry` / `subagent_registry` records + `LedgerSnapshotDeduper` skips byte-identical snapshots at the write site - `model_request_summary`: per-message summaries capped (newest 64 messages / 256 KB budget); older messages degrade to role+chars stubs — record still describes the whole request - `JsonlSessionStorage._openLocked`: stat-first, refuse >2 GiB with a named `tooLarge` `SessionException` pointing at windowed resume / `fa session repair`; ranged filesystems get a fully streamed line-scan parse with header-only decode of giant `custom` ledgers (only the latest per `customType` is fully parsed — exactly what resume rehydration reads) - `session_repair.dart` + CLI: drop replay-only ledger types, keep-latest for snapshot registries, conservative (unknown/unparseable lines kept), backup + `--dry-run` ### How to verify ```bash dart test test/session test/trajectory test/task test/cli ``` Full core suite (`dart test --exclude-tags integration`): 7960 passed / 16 skipped. The 3 failures in `providers_queue_editor_test.dart` are environmental — the CI shell leaks `FA_PROVIDERS_QUEUE`, which the editor correctly refuses to override (all 13 pass with the var unset). A pre-existing glibc heap-corruption abort in the PTY-harness teardown also reproduces on the base commit and is unrelated.
Architecture diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD OPEN[Session open] --> STAT[fileInfo stat] STAT -->|> 2 GiB| REFUSE[tooLarge SessionException] REFUSE --> HINT[windowed resume / fa session repair] STAT -->|<= 2 GiB| STREAM[streamed line scan
bounded chunks] STREAM --> HDR[header-only decode
of giant custom ledgers] HDR --> LATEST[fully parse latest
record per customType] WRITE[ledger writes] --> CAP[ledger_caps: 300-char field cap] CAP --> DEDUP[skip identical snapshots] REPAIR[fa session repair] --> REWRITE[drop replay-only ledgers

# pr-1247: gh-1073 Session JSONL grows unboundedly (12 GiB ledger records) → resume fails with 'Failed to read session' + heap-exhaustion crash ## Description ### What changed Bounded the session-JSONL growth that grew a month-long session to 12.4 GiB and made open/resume safe for huge files: ledger payloads are capped and deduped at the write site, the full open streams the file in bounded chunks (never one giant `String`) with a 2 GiB hard backstop, and a new `fa session repair` command rewrites bloated JSONLs. This leg fixed the last review leftovers: one analyzer lint and two stale retry-test assertions that still counted the old `readTextFile` open surface (the open now stats + streams, so the counters read `statCalls`). ### Key decisions - `ledger_caps.dart`: 300-char cap on every string field in `shell_job_registry` / `subagent_registry` records + `LedgerSnapshotDeduper` skips byte-identical snapshots at the write site - `model_request_summary`: per-message summaries capped (newest 64 messages / 256 KB budget); older messages degrade to role+chars stubs — record still describes the whole request - `JsonlSessionStorage._openLocked`: stat-first, refuse >2 GiB with a named `tooLarge` `SessionException` pointing at windowed resume / `fa session repair`; ranged filesystems get a fully streamed line-scan parse with header-only decode of giant `custom` ledgers (only the latest per `customType` is fully parsed — exactly what resume rehydration reads) - `session_repair.dart` + CLI: drop replay-only ledger types, keep-latest for snapshot registries, conservative (unknown/unparseable lines kept), backup + `--dry-run` ### How to verify ```bash dart test test/session test/trajectory test/task test/cli ``` Full core suite (`dart test --exclude-tags integration`): 7960 passed / 16 skipped. The 3 failures in `providers_queue_editor_test.dart` are environmental — the CI shell leaks `FA_PROVIDERS_QUEUE`, which the editor correctly refuses to override (all 13 pass with the var unset). A pre-existing glibc heap-corruption abort in the PTY-harness teardown also reproduces on the base commit and is unrelated.
Architecture diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD OPEN[Session open] --> STAT[fileInfo stat] STAT -->|> 2 GiB| REFUSE[tooLarge SessionException] REFUSE --> HINT[windowed resume / fa session repair] STAT -->|<= 2 GiB| STREAM[streamed line scan
bounded chunks] STREAM --> HDR[header-only decode
of giant custom ledgers] HDR --> LATEST[fully parse latest
record per customType] WRITE[ledger writes] --> CAP[ledger_caps: 300-char field cap] CAP --> DEDUP[skip identical snapshots] REPAIR[fa session repair] --> REWRITE[drop replay-only ledgers
keep-latest registries + backup] ```

The by-id branch below correctly refuses to repair a session with a fresh presence heartbeat ("repairing under a writer loses appends"), and both this file's doc comment and the `cli_help.dart` entry promise "A live session (fresh heartbeat) is refused" unconditionally. But when the target ends in `.jsonl`, this branch takes `path = target` and **never checks presence** — `fa session repair /live/session.jsonl` on a running session will scan, rewrite, and swap the file under the writer, silently dropping every append between the scan and the rename.

The fix is cheap: run the same `presenceStore` lookup for the path branch. Resolving a path to a session id would need a listing scan, but even a simpler guard helps — e.g. refuse when *any* fresh heartbeat row names this path, or at minimum rename the option/document it as an unsafe expert escape hatch. As written, the doc comment overpromises and the most dangerous input shape is the least protected one.

{"content":"💡 **SUGGESTION: the board snapshot is serialized twice, and the deduper marks state persisted before the write succeeds**

Two small things in this hunk:

1. `_jobBoard.toRecords()` is called twice and the payload is JSON-encoded twice — once here for the dedupe key, once inside `appendCustomEntry`. With the new 50-card cap that's cheap, but `final records = _jobBoard.toRecords(); final json = jsonEncode(records);` makes the dedupe key honestly match what gets written.
2. `LedgerSnapshotDeduper.shouldPersist` advances `_lastJson` before the append runs. The chain's `.catchError` swallows append failures by design — but then the deduper believes the snapshot persisted, so the retried *identical* snapshot is skipped and the ledger silently misses a state until the next mutation. Consider rolling the deduper back on write failure (e.g. `shouldPersist` returning a token the catch path can restore), or documenting the at-most-one-lost-snapshot window.

# Pull Request Information - **PR #**: 1247 - **URL**: https://github.com/IstiN/flutter_agent_harness/pull/1247 - **Title**: gh-1073 Session JSONL grows unboundedly (12 GiB ledger records) → resume fails with 'Failed to read session' + heap-exhaustion crash - **Author**: ai-teammate - **Branch**: `ai/gh-1073` → `main` - **State**: open - **Files Changed**: 29 - **Additions**: +4680 - **Deletions**: -60 - **Created**: 2026-10-04T21:28:28Z - **Updated**: 2026-10-04T22:14:31Z ## PR Description ### What changed Bounded the session-JSONL growth that grew a month-long session to 12.4 GiB and made open/resume safe for huge files: ledger payloads are capped and deduped at the write site, the full open streams the file in bounded chunks (never one giant `String`) with a 2 GiB hard backstop, and a new `fa session repair` command rewrites bloated JSONLs. This leg fixed the last review leftovers: one analyzer lint and two stale retry-test assertions that still counted the old `readTextFile` open surface (the open now stats + streams, so the counters read `statCalls`). ### Key decisions - `ledger_caps.dart`: 300-char cap on every string field in `shell_job_registry` / `subagent_registry` records + `LedgerSnapshotDeduper` skips byte-identical snapshots at the write site - `model_request_summary`: per-message summaries capped (newest 64 messages / 256 KB budget); older messages degrade to role+chars stubs — record still describes the whole request - `JsonlSessionStorage._openLocked`: stat-first, refuse >2 GiB with a named `tooLarge` `SessionException` pointing at windowed resume / `fa session repair`; ranged filesystems get a fully streamed line-scan parse with header-only decode of giant `custom` ledgers (only the latest per `customType` is fully parsed — exactly what resume rehydration reads) - `session_repair.dart` + CLI: drop replay-only ledger types, keep-latest for snapshot registries, conservative (unknown/unparseable lines kept), backup + `--dry-run` ### How to verify ```bash dart test test/session test/trajectory test/task test/cli ``` Full core suite (`dart test --exclude-tags integration`): 7960 passed / 16 skipped. The 3 failures in `providers_queue_editor_test.dart` are environmental — the CI shell leaks `FA_PROVIDERS_QUEUE`, which the editor correctly refuses to override (all 13 pass with the var unset). A pre-existing glibc heap-corruption abort in the PTY-harness teardown also reproduces on the base commit and is unrelated.
Architecture diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD OPEN[Session open] --> STAT[fileInfo stat] STAT -->|> 2 GiB| REFUSE[tooLarge SessionException] REFUSE --> HINT[windowed resume / fa session repair] STAT -->|<= 2 GiB| STREAM[streamed line scan
bounded chunks] STREAM --> HDR[header-only decode
of giant custom ledgers] HDR --> LATEST[fully parse latest
record per customType] WRITE[ledger writes] --> CAP[ledger_caps: 300-char field cap] CAP --> DEDUP[skip identical snapshots] REPAIR[fa session repair] --> REWRITE[drop replay-only ledgers
keep-latest registries + backup] ```

content.text:
# Review — PR #1247

## Summary
The gh-1073 session-JSONL work itself is solid: write-site caps + dedup, streamed line-scan open with a 2 GiB backstop, header-only decode of giant ledger records, conservative `fa session repair` with backup/dry-run, and good new tests (19 new session tests pass locally). **However, the branch's merge of `main` (gh-1232's `bin/fah.dart` → part-file split) was resolved by reinstating the branch's old monolithic `bin/fah.dart`, which drops the `part` directives and three imports.** That leaves six orphaned `part of` files (599 analyzer errors → both CI `dart analyze` steps fail), silently kills `fa jsr` and `fa wire-serve`, and unwires the gh-1000 boot-restore pin — `test/bin_boot_restore_pin_test.dart` fails on this head (verified locally: 4 passed / 1 failed). The PR description's "7960 passed" claim is not true of the current head.

## Key Issues
- 🚨 `bin/fah.dart` merge damage: orphaned part files (`dart analyze` red), `fa jsr` / `fa wire-serve` handlers dead, `resolveBootFolderPin` no longer called (2 BLOCKING)
- ⚠️ `fa session repair <path>.jsonl` skips the live-session guard the by-id path enforces — repairing under a live writer silently loses appends (1 IMPORTANT)
- 💡 Backup overwrite on repeated repair, `ledgetTextCapChars` typo, double board serialization, `.corrupt` sidecar double newline, `test/dbg_heal_test.dart` debug leftover with zero assertions (5 SUGGESTION)

## Next Steps
1. Re-resolve the `bin/fah.dart` merge: keep main's part-file structure (or delete the part files wholesale and port their content forward, including jsr/wire-serve/boot-restore wiring), then re-run `dart analyze` and `test/bin_boot_restore_pin_test.dart`.
2. Extend the live-session presence check to the direct-`.jsonl`-path branch of `runSessionRepairCliCommand` (or explicitly document path mode as an unsafe escape hatch).
3. Sweep the suggestion-level items; none block merge once the two blockers land.

# Pull Request Information - **PR #**: 1247 - **URL**: https://github.com/IstiN/flutter_agent_harness/pull/1247 - **Title**: gh-1073 Session JSONL grows unboundedly (12 GiB ledger records) → resume fails with 'Failed to read session' + heap-exhaustion crash - **Author**: ai-teammate - **Branch**: `ai/gh-1073` → `main` - **State**: open - **Files Changed**: 29 - **Additions**: +4680 - **Deletions**: -60 - **Created**: 2026-10-04T21:28:28Z - **Updated**: 2026-10-04T22:14:31Z ## PR Description ### What changed Bounded the session-JSONL growth that grew a month-long session to 12.4 GiB and made open/resume safe for huge files: ledger payloads are capped and deduped at the write site, the full open streams the file in bounded chunks (never one giant `String`) with a 2 GiB hard backstop, and a new `fa session repair` command rewrites bloated JSONLs. This leg fixed the last review leftovers: one analyzer lint and two stale retry-test assertions that still counted the old `readTextFile` open surface (the open now stats + streams, so the counters read `statCalls`). ### Key decisions - `ledger_caps.dart`: 300-char cap on every string field in `shell_job_registry` / `subagent_registry` records + `LedgerSnapshotDeduper` skips byte-identical snapshots at the write site - `model_request_summary`: per-message summaries capped (newest 64 messages / 256 KB budget); older messages degrade to role+chars stubs — record still describes the whole request - `JsonlSessionStorage._openLocked`: stat-first, refuse >2 GiB with a named `tooLarge` `SessionException` pointing at windowed resume / `fa session repair`; ranged filesystems get a fully streamed line-scan parse with header-only decode of giant `custom` ledgers (only the latest per `customType` is fully parsed — exactly what resume rehydration reads) - `session_repair.dart` + CLI: drop replay-only ledger types, keep-latest for snapshot registries, conservative (unknown/unparseable lines kept), backup + `--dry-run` ### How to verify ```bash dart test test/session test/trajectory test/task test/cli ``` Full core suite (`dart test --exclude-tags integration`): 7960 passed / 16 skipped. The 3 failures in `providers_queue_editor_test.dart` are environmental — the CI shell leaks `FA_PROVIDERS_QUEUE`, which the editor correctly refuses to override (all 13 pass with the var unset). A pre-existing glibc heap-corruption abort in the PTY-harness teardown also reproduces on the base commit and is unrelated.

# Review — PR #1247

## Summary
The gh-1073 session-JSONL work itself is solid: write-site caps + dedup, streamed line-scan open with a 2 GiB backstop, header-only decode of giant ledger records, conservative `fa session repair` with backup/dry-run, and good new tests (19 new session tests pass locally). **However, the branch's merge of `main` (gh-1232's `bin/fah.dart` → part-file split) was resolved by reinstating the branch's old monolithic `bin/fah.dart`, which drops the `part` directives and three imports.** That leaves six orphaned `part of` files (599 analyzer errors → both CI `dart analyze` steps fail), silently kills `fa jsr` and `fa wire-serve`, and unwires the gh-1000 boot-restore pin — `test/bin_boot_restore_pin_test.dart` fails on this head (verified locally: 4 passed / 1 failed). The PR description's "7960 passed" claim is not true of the current head.

## Key Issues
- 🚨 `bin/fah.dart` merge damage: orphaned part files (`dart analyze` red), `fa jsr` / `fa wire-serve` handlers dead, `resolveBootFolderPin` no longer called (2 BLOCKING)
- ⚠️ `fa session repair <path>.jsonl` skips the live-session guard the by-id path enforces — repairing under a live writer silently loses appends (1 IMPORTANT)
- 💡 Backup overwrite on repeated repair, `ledgetTextCapChars` typo, double board serialization, `.corrupt` sidecar double newline, `test/dbg_heal_test.dart` debug leftover with zero assertions (5 SUGGESTION)

## Next Steps
1. Re-resolve the `bin/fah.dart` merge: keep main's part-file structure (or delete the part files wholesale and port their content forward, including jsr/wire-serve/boot-restore wiring), then re-run `dart analyze` and `test/bin_boot_restore_pin_test.dart`.
2. Extend the live-session presence check to the direct-`.jsonl`-path branch of `runSessionRepairCliCommand` (or explicitly document path mode as an unsafe escape hatch).
3. Sweep the suggestion-level items; none block merge once the two blockers land.

Do not ask for identifiers; the context is already available locally. ```mermaid flowchart TD G1["⚠️ Review Guidelines — evaluate against existing codebase patterns"] G2["Before reviewing, explore the project's code structure, architecture, and testing patterns"] G3["If AGENTS.md exists → READ it — defines coding styles to check against"] G4["Flag deviations from established patterns unless justified in PR description"] G1 --> G2 --> G3 --> G4 ``` # PR Review General Guidelines ## Review flow ```mermaid flowchart TD START([PR ready for review]) --> READ["1. Test coverage · Duplication · Backward compatibility"] DIMS --> SEVERITY["6. Classify each finding:
BLOCKING / IMPORTANT / SUGGESTION"] SEVERITY --> EXHAUST["7. Exhaustive pass:
re-read changed files,
surface ALL remaining issues"] EXHAUST --> OUTPUT["8. Write outputs:
pr_review.json · pr_review_general.md · pr_review_comments/*.md"] OUTPUT --> END([End]) ``` ## 1. Input context — MANDATORY reading order ```mermaid flowchart TD subgraph PR_CONTEXT["⚠️ PR-specific files (read first)"] P1["1️⃣ instruction.md (repo root) — project stack, conventions"] P2["2️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_info.md — PR title, author, branch, description"] P3["3️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_diff.txt — the diff to review"] P4["4️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_files.txt — list of changed files"] P5["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures.md — CI failures = BLOCKING (last 500 lines)"] P5_FULL["5️⃣ input/TICKET/ci_failures_full.log — full CI logs"] P6["6️⃣ input/TICKET/pr_discussions.md + pr_discussions_raw.json — existing comments"] P1 --> P2 --> P3 --> P4 --> P5 --> P5_FULL --> P6 end subgraph TICKET_CONTEXT["Ticket context (for understanding PR purpose)"] T1["7️⃣ input/TICKET/ticket.md — linked ticket description, ACs"] T2["8️⃣ input/TICKET/comments.md — ticket discussion if present"] T3["9️⃣ input/TICKET/parent-*.md — parent story context"] T4["🔟 input/TICKET/confluence/*.md — linked specifications"] T1 --> T2 --> T3 --> T4 end subgraph RULE["⚠️ Rule"] R1["If file exists in input/ → read locally, do NOT re-fetch via dmtools"] end PR_CONTEXT --> TICKET_CONTEXT --> RULE ``` Read PR files to understand WHAT changed. Read ticket files to understand WHY it changed and verify against requirements. ## 2. Diff checklist — apply to `pr_diff.txt` For every hunk, ask at least these questions: - [ ] Does the change match the ticket scope? Any scope creep? - [ ] Are new or changed public APIs contract-safe for existing callers? - [ ] Is user/external input validated, sanitized, or escaped? - [ ] Are secrets, tokens, or PATs handled safely — not logged, not interpolated into shell scripts? - [ ] Are new or modified files present under `testing/` in a non-test-automation PR? - [ ] Is dead code, unused imports, or obvious duplication introduced? - [ ] Are error paths handled, or are failures silently swallowed? - [ ] Are new dependencies justified and compatible with the existing stack? - [ ] Beyond blockers: what other maintainability, correctness, or quality improvements are visible in the changed code? ## 3. Changed-file deep read Do not review from the diff alone. Read the full content of every changed file: - imports and dependencies - class/method responsibilities and adherence to SRP / OOP principles - naming consistency with the rest of the codebase - error handling, logging, and edge cases - test coverage for changed behavior - backward-compatibility and migration impact ## 4. Impact analysis (CodeGraph or grep fallback) Use CodeGraph to find "what could break": - `codegraph_callers` / `codegraph_callees` on modified public symbols - `codegraph_search` for: `PAT_TOKEN`, `secrets.`, `github.token`, `previousViewModel` - `codegraph_impact` before flagging architectural changes **If CodeGraph unavailable**, use grep and document it: ```bash grep -rn "changedFunctionName" --include="*.ts" . grep -rn "secrets\.\|github\.token" . ``` ## 5. Review dimensions Rate the PR across all relevant dimensions: | Dimension | What to check | |---|---| | **Security** | injection, unsafe interpolation, secret leakage, missing permissions, unsafe defaults | | **Architecture / OOP** | SRP, coupling, abstraction consistency, provider/repository boundaries | | **Code quality** | naming, complexity, error handling, logging, comments | | **Tests** | coverage for new/changed paths, meaningful assertions, no brittle string-only tests | | **Duplication** | copy-paste, duplicated logic across files, duplicated configuration | | **Backward compatibility** | public API changes, migration paths, default behavior | | **Performance** | unnecessary rebuilds, heavy sync operations, missing timeouts | | **Workflow / CI safety** | (when `.github/workflows/` changes) secret declarations, ref pinning, permissions, timeouts | ## 6. Severity classification Classify every finding before writing outputs: - **BLOCKING** — merge would cause a bug, security issue, data loss, or CI break. Must be fixed. - **IMPORTANT** — real maintainability or correctness issue. Strongly prefer fixing before merge. - **SUGGESTION** — optional improvement, style, or future polish. Does not block merge. When in doubt, start one level higher; downgrade only after confirming the risk is negligible. ## 7. Exhaustive single-pass review Treat **every** review as the final and only review pass. The author will not get another chance to catch missed findings cheaply. - Do not defer SUGGESTION or IMPORTANT items to a later round because a BLOCKING issue exists. - After classifying all findings, re-read every changed file and ask: *"What else is improvable here?"* - Before writing outputs, verify that no obvious quality, maintainability, or correctness issue was left unreported. - Aim to surface the maximum number of actionable findings in this single iteration. ## 8. Outputs Write the standard review artifacts: - `outputs/pr_review.json` — structured data with `recommendation`, `summary`, `inlineComments`, `issueCounts` - `outputs/pr_review_general.md` — 1-2 paragraph general PR comment - `outputs/pr_review_comments/*.md` — one file per detailed inline comment **Inline comment lines must be present in the PR diff.** GitHub review threads can only be attached to added or context lines inside a diff hunk. # Pull Request Information - **PR #**: 1247 - **URL**: https://github.com/IstiN/flutter_agent_harness/pull/1247 - **Title**: gh-1073 Session JSONL grows unboundedly (12 GiB ledger records) → resume fails with 'Failed to read session' + heap-exhaustion crash - **Author**: ai-teammate - **Branch**: `ai/gh-1073` → `main` - **State**: open - **Files Changed**: 29 - **Additions**: +4680 - **Deletions**: -60 - **Created**: 2026-10-04T21:28:28Z - **Updated**: 2026-10-04T22:14:31Z ## PR Description ### What changed Bounded the session-JSONL growth that grew a month-long session to 12.4 GiB and made open/resume safe for huge files: ledger payloads are capped and deduped at the write site, the full open streams the file in bounded chunks (never one giant `String`) with a 2 GiB hard backstop, and a new `fa session repair` command rewrites bloated JSONLs. This leg fixed the last review leftovers: one analyzer lint and two stale retry-test assertions that still counted the old `readTextFile` open surface (the open now stats + streams, so the counters read `statCalls`). ### Key decisions - `ledger_caps.dart`: 300-char cap on every string field in `shell_job_registry` / `subagent_registry` records + `LedgerSnapshotDeduper` skips byte-identical snapshots at the write site - `model_request_summary`: per-message summaries capped (newest 64 messages / 256 KB budget); older messages degrade to role+chars stubs — record still describes the whole request - `JsonlSessionStorage._openLocked`: stat-first, refuse >2 GiB with a named `tooLarge` `SessionException` pointing at windowed resume / `fa session repair`; ranged filesystems get a fully streamed line-scan parse with header-only decode of giant `custom` ledgers (only the latest per `customType` is fully parsed — exactly what resume rehydration reads) - `session_repair.dart` + CLI: drop replay-only ledger types, keep-latest for snapshot registries, conservative (unknown/unparseable lines kept), backup + `--dry-run` ### How to verify ```bash dart test test/session test/trajectory test/task test/cli ``` Full core suite (`dart test --exclude-tags integration`): 7960 passed / 16 skipped. The 3 failures in `providers_queue_editor_test.dart` are environmental — the CI shell leaks `FA_PROVIDERS_QUEUE`, which the editor correctly refuses to override (all 13 pass with the var unset). A pre-existing glibc heap-corruption abort in the PTY-harness teardown also reproduces on the base commit and is unrelated.
Architecture diagram ```mermaid flowchart TD OPEN[Session open] --> STAT[fileInfo stat] STAT -->|> 2 GiB| REFUSE[tooLarge SessionException] REFUSE --> HINT[windowed resume / fa session repair] STAT -->|<= 2 GiB| STREAM[streamed line scan
bounded chunks] STREAM --> HDR[header-only decode
of giant custom ledgers] HDR --> LATEST[fully parse latest
record per customType] WRITE[ledger writes] --> CAP[ledger_caps: 300-char field cap] CAP --> DEDUP[skip identical snapshots] REPAIR[fa session repair] --> REWRITE[drop replay-only ledgers
keep-latest registries + backup] ```

# pr-1247: gh-1073 Session JSONL grows unboundedly (12 GiB ledger records) → resume fails with 'Failed to read session' + heap-exhaustion crash ## Description ### What changed Bounded the session-JSONL growth that grew a month-long session to 12.4 GiB and made open/resume safe for huge files: ledger payloads are capped and deduped at the write site, the full open streams the file in bounded chunks (never one giant `String`) with a 2 GiB hard backstop, and a new `fa session repair` command rewrites bloated JSONLs. This leg fixed the last review leftovers: one analyzer lint and two stale retry-test assertions that still counted the old `readTextFile` open surface (the open now stats + streams, so the counters read `statCalls`). ### Key decisions - `ledger_caps.dart`: 300-char cap on every string field in `shell_job_registry` / `subagent_registry` records + `LedgerSnapshotDeduper` skips byte-identical snapshots at the write site - `model_request_summary`: per-message summaries capped (newest 64 messages / 256 KB budget); older messages degrade to role+chars stubs — record still describes the whole request - `JsonlSessionStorage._openLocked`: stat-first, refuse >2 GiB with a named `tooLarge` `SessionException` pointing at windowed resume / `fa session repair`; ranged filesystems get a fully streamed line-scan parse with header-only decode of giant `custom` ledgers (only the latest per `customType` is fully parsed — exactly what resume rehydration reads) - `session_repair.dart` + CLI: drop replay-only ledger types, keep-latest for snapshot registries, conservative (unknown/unparseable lines kept), backup + `--dry-run` ### How to verify ```bash dart test test/session test/trajectory test/task test/cli ``` Full core suite (`dart test --exclude-tags integration`): 7960 passed / 16 skipped. The 3 failures in `providers_queue_editor_test.dart` are environmental — the CI shell leaks `FA_PROVIDERS_QUEUE`, which the editor correctly refuses to override (all 13 pass with the var unset). A pre-existing glibc heap-corruption abort in the PTY-harness teardown also reproduces on the base commit and is unrelated.

bounded chunks] STREAM --> HDR[header-only decode

record per customType] WRITE[ledger writes] --> CAP[ledger_caps: 300-char field cap] CAP --> DEDUP[skip identical snapshots] REPAIR[fa session repair] --> REWRITE[drop replay-only ledgers
keep-latest registries + backup] ```

## Summary
The gh-1073 session-JSONL work itself is solid: write-site caps + dedup, streamed line-scan open with a 2 GiB backstop, header-only decode of giant ledger records, conservative `fa session repair` with backup/dry-run, and good new tests (19 new session tests pass locally). **However, the branch's merge of `main` (gh-1232's `bin/fah.dart` → part-file split) was resolved by reinstating the branch's old monolithic `bin/fah.dart`, which drops the `part` directives and three imports.** That leaves six orphaned `part of` files (599 analyzer errors → both CI `dart analyze` steps fail), silently kills `fa jsr` and `fa wire-serve`, and unwires the gh-1000 boot-restore pin — `test/bin_boot_restore_pin_test.dart` fails on this head (verified locally: 4 passed / 1 failed). The PR description's "7960 passed" claim is not true of the current head.

2. Extend the live-session presence check to the direct-`.jsonl`-path branch of `runSessionRepairCliCommand` (or explicitly document path mode as an unsafe escape hatch).
3. Sweep the suggestion-level items; none block merge once the two blockers land.
